title: Transient instruction priority playbook (scratch)
content:
Purpose:
- Capture a lightweight design for transient (short-lived) instruction overlays that clients can push with explicit priority and TTL. Ideas are for a client-side / session-side mechanism that allows temporary, preemptive instructions (e.g., `tone: terse`, `avoid-topics: finance`, `safety-strict: true`) to be honored for a bounded number of requests or time window without mutating the canonical system prompt.

Background and motivation (notes):
- Common pattern: product features need to nudge model behavior for a few turns (e.g., ephemeral user preference, ad-hoc regulatory mode, test harness toggles).
- We must avoid persisting these permanently into session state or model-anchored system prompts.
- Needs to play nicely with caching, batching, KV cache reuse, and rollbacks/fallbacks when capacity or compatibility changes.

Goals:
- Simple client API to attach transient instructions to a request or session with scoped TTL and priority.
- Deterministic precedence rules when multiple instruction sources exist (session-level, route defaults, per-request transient).
- Efficient for the runtime: minimal tokenization/serialization overhead, compatible with prefix caching and partial KV reuse.
- Observability: per-instruction telemetry (applied/ignored/evicted) for diagnostics and evals.

Non-goals:
- Full policy engine or long-term storage of preferences. (Those belong in Tenant profile or persistent session objects.)

Sketch: API shapes (HTTP / SDK level)
1) POST add transient instruction to session (client side):
   POST /v1/sessions/{session_id}/transient-instructions
   body (application/json):
   {
     "instruction_id": "cli-20241012-01",
     "payload": "system: You are concise and factual.",
     "priority": 75,            // 0-100 integer; higher wins
     "scope": "session",      // request | session | tenant (use tenant sparingly)
     "ttl_seconds": 30,        // soft TTL in seconds
     "max_uses": 5,            // optional: max number of requests it can be applied to
     "preempt": true,          // if true, can override lower-priority system prompts
     "metadata": {"origin": "client-ui:quick-mode"} // freeform string map (stringified client-side)
   }

2) Per-request attachment (one-off):
   POST /v1/generate (usual generate endpoint)
   add header: X-Transient-Instruction: cli-20241012-01  OR include body field transient_instruction: { ... inline payload ... }

Server-side semantics (draft):
- Instruction store: ephemeral, in-memory store keyed by session_id -> list(sorted by priority then created_at). Items have expires_at and remaining_uses.
- On request ingress, runtime compiles the effective prompt by merging in this precedence order (higher index wins):
   1) Route-declared required system instruction (immutable)
   2) Tenant defaults / account policies (if scope==tenant and allowed)
   3) Session persistent instructions (long-lived session metadata)
   4) Transient instructions (sorted by priority, ties by newest-first if preempt true)
   5) Request-level transient (if present)
- If a transient instruction has preempt=true and conflicts with a higher-priority persistent system prompt, we allow a configurable override policy (default: false). That policy must be audited and require tenant opt-in.

Interactions with caching & batching:
- Goal: avoid tokenizing transient instructions every time if unchanged across requests in a batch.
- Memoization key: session_id + instruction_set_hash + model+max_tokens+route. The runtime can reuse prefix tokenization for identical instruction sets.
- When instruction set differs between grouped requests, runtime should fall back to separate generation paths (no unsafe token reuse).
- If instruction includes non-deterministic placeholders (e.g., timestamp), treat as unique (no cache).

ASCII architecture diagram (very rough):
   [Client] --(API call + optional transient instruction)--> [Ingress / Edge] -- lookup session->transient-store --> [Routing] --> [Serving runtime workers]
                                              |
                                              +-- telemetry: TI_APPLIED / TI_IGNORED / TI_EVICTED

Eviction policies & lifespan notes:
- TTL expiry (wall-clock) and max_uses both enforced. Whichever comes first ends the instruction.
- Memory pressure eviction: LRU across sessions, but favor eviction of lowest-priority items first.
- Manual revocation: POST /v1/sessions/{id}/transient-instructions/{instruction_id}:delete

Data model (proto/json sketch - inline for clarity):
- Because top-level JSON required in this doc, below is shown as a stringified JSON example (runtime will use small proto in practice):
   {"instruction_id":"cli-20241012-01","payload":"system: be terse","priority":"75","scope":"session","ttl_seconds":"30","max_uses":"5","preempt":"true","created_at":"2024-10-12T14:32:00Z"}

Telemetry & metrics (what to track):
- TI_CREATED (counts), TI_APPLIED, TI_IGNORED(reason), TI_EXPIRY, TI_EVICTED(reason), TI_REVOCATION
- Latency delta when transient present vs absent (tokenize cost / compilation cost)
- Cache hit ratio for instruction-set tokenization
- Per-instruction usage histogram (how many requests used before expiry)

Rollout experiment plan (A/B):
- Phase A: client-side only (clients send a header; server ignores, it is logged) -> capture real usage patterns
- Phase B: server honors low-risk transient flags (non-preemptive) for 10% of traffic; collect TI_APPLIED metrics, check evals for regressions
- Phase C: enable preemptive for opt-in tenants + add audit logs and policy checks

Security & abuse considerations:
- Preemptive overrides are powerful: require tenant-level opt-in + audit trail + bounded TTL with lower upper-bound for unknown tenants.
- Limit instruction length (token cap) and remove ability to inject function-calls or tool spec into transient payloads unless tenant explicitly allows.
- Rate limit TI creation per session and per tenant to avoid instruction spam.

Open questions / TODOs:
- How to represent composable priorities when we want to *merge* structured instructions (e.g., two instructions that set disjoint keys)? Current model is last-writer wins per conflict key, but we should explore a key-level merge model.
- Should TTL be soft (server may extend while active) or strict? For now prefer strict for predictability.
- UI affordances: should SDK expose an optimistic local-apply that updates UI even before server ack? UX tradeoffs.
- Backward compatibility with existing session-serialization formats (see model-versioning-runtime/api notes).

Small example flows (quick):
1) Quick-mode toggle
   - Client creates transient instruction payload: {"payload":"system: be concise; tone: terse","priority":60,"ttl_seconds":120}
   - UI sets header and sends generate requests. Server applies for next N requests, expires after 2 minutes.

2) Safety override during a demo (opt-in tenant only)
   - Higher priority preempt=true, ttl_seconds=15, max_uses=1. After one request it is auto-removed and recorded in audit log.

Implementation checklist (engineering):
- [ ] Small in-memory transient store and APIs (create/list/delete) behind ingress.
- [ ] Prefix-tokenization cache keyed on instruction_set_hash.
- [ ] Telemetry events (TI_*) and a dashboard slice in Console (per-tenant).
- [ ] SDK helpers (ts/python) to attach/invalidate transient instructions.
- [ ] Policy gate for preemptive overrides + opt-in flow.
- [ ] Load test: create many short-lived instructions, validate eviction behavior and memory usage.

Notes-to-self / scribbles:
- Keep the proto small: instruction payload (string), small flags. No huge metadata blobs.
- Consider signed instruction tokens for untrusted clients (so edge can validate origin) — but that adds complexity; maybe v2.
- For experiments, correlate TI_APPLIED with quality regressions in eval harness (run prompt-set with and without TI applied).

References / similar ideas seen elsewhere in drive: session-handshake, ephemeral-client-policy-dsl, prompt-orchestration-rulebook; but this is purposefully narrower: ephemeral *instructions* not session-state.

End of scratchpad. Will formalize into short PRD if prototype results are promising.
